newsitem.title: USA: China accused as U.S. campaign funds probe opens.
newsitem.headline: China accused as U.S. campaign funds probe opens.

text.p: A Senate probe into possible violations of electoral campaign funding laws opened on Tuesday with a dramatic allegation that China planned to use substantial sums of money to influence American politics.

The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee hearing was also told that John Huang, a key figure in allegations of funding abuses in President Bill Clinton's 1996 campaign, had agreed to testify if given limited immunity against prosecution.

Committee chairman Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican, began the long-awaited televised hearings with a statement that Beijing's communist leaders had a plan to build political influence in the United States.
"The committee believes that high-level Chinese government officials crafted a plan to increase China's influence over the U.S. political process," he said.

Thompson said the plan was drawn up to respond to advances by Taiwan in building influence in Washington and included "typical appropriate" measures for foreign states such as hiring lobbyists and diplomatic visits.

"However, other parts of the plan direct actions that are illegal under U.S. law. Although most discussion of the plan focuses on Congress our investigation suggests it affected the 1996 presidential race and state elections as well," he said.

Thompson, repeating allegations made in the media or under investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, said China "is believed to have allocated substantial sums of money to achieve its objectives."

He said Beijing had shown an interest in "developing long-term relationships with persons it has identified as up-and-coming officials at state and local levels. The intent is to establish relations that can be cultivated as the officials rise through the ranks to higher office."

The leading Democrat on the committee, Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, warned against a "jump to conclusions," asking: "Is there any real evidence that the Chinese government, or any other foreign government, actually infiltrated the American government via campaign contributions?"
Glenn, quoting news reports that said China planned to use about $2 million to gain influence by focusing on Congress, said the only known lobbying activity by China was legitimate.

Thompson said Clinton's decision to grant a visa to Taiwan's President Lee Teng-hui to visit his former college, Cornell University, in 1996 after pressure from Congress caught Beijing "off-guard" and led to its decision to step up its involvement in U.S. politics.

The hearing will initially investigate a tangled web of allegedly illegal foreign contributions to Clinton's 1996 campaign, predominantly through Asians or Asian Americans, and possible improper use of the White House to solicit funds.

Thompson said they would also look into allegations of money-laundering, influence-peddling, violations of conflict of interest laws and questions on whether U.S. domestic and foreign policies were affected by political contributions.
"The allegations before us are serious. ... These matters go to the basic integrity of our governent and our electoral process," he said.

Democrats have also called for Republican party officials to testify on allegations they received possibly improper contributions from Asian donors and Glenn used his opening statement to detail allegations of Republican violations.

He announced that Huang, a former Commerce Department official who became an important Democratic party fundraiser, had said he would be prepared to appear before the committee provided he be given limited immunity.

The Ohio democrat said Huang would still be open to criminal prosecution on a variety of charges if there were evidence he committed espionage, disclosed classified information or made false statements under oath.
Thompson said the offer would be considered as the hearing proceeded.

The Democratic National Committee returned nearly $1.6 million in questionable funds raised by Huang. Another important fund-raising figure, Charles Yah Lin Trie, a former Arkansas restaurateur and friend of Clinton, remains in hiding and is believed to be in China. He raised or donated $645,000 for Democrats which was later returned.
